Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:68: Further, one must be careful, while occupied with Torah, not to interrupt it with conversation, for this is like mixing the profane with something holy, and its punishment is severe - as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shelach Lecha, page 162a), that a heavenly voice says three things in the Garden of Eden every day, before Bezalel begins to reveal the secrets of the wise, and one of them is, whoever interrupts shall be interrupted - explained as: whoever interrupts words of Torah for idle words, his life shall be interrupted from this world, and his judgment stands in that world - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:69: And this is what they said in the chapter "Ein Dorshin" (Chagigah 8b): Rabbi Levi said, whoever interrupts words of Torah and occupies himself with idle conversation is fed the coals of broom, as it is said (Job 30:4), "who pluck saltwort by the bushes, and the roots of broom are their food" - and Rashi, peace be upon him, explained in Tractate Avodah Zarah, first chapter (3b), that "who interrupts for idle conversation" - "saltwort" [maluach] is words of moisture, and essentially, another interpretation, "written on tablets." And "coals of broom" was explained in the previous chapter, in the name of Rashi, peace be upon him, concerning the matter of (Psalms 120:4), "sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of broom" - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:70: And the reason for this is that the Torah is fire, and was given in fire, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:2), "from His right hand went a fiery law for them" - and speaking idle words is fiery coals, for speech comes from the fire of the heart, and when a person is occupied with Torah, his voice hews flames of fire in holiness - however, when he is occupied with idle conversation, it is a foreign fire, and therefore, "in his net which he hid, his own foot is caught" - by the fire of blemish, fire shall consume him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:71: And in the reason for "whoever interrupts, and so on," is because the Torah is your life and the length of your days - your life in this world, and length of days in the World to Come (cf. Tanchuma, Shemini 11) - and therefore, measure for measure, he has a punishment in this world and in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:72: And when a person, in his occupation with Torah, places the fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, before him, he shall not come to interrupt - as they said, of blessed memory, in Midrash Eichah, on the verse (Lamentations 2:19), "pour out your heart like water before the presence of the LORD," in these words: any Torah scholar who sits alone by himself and reads and studies, it is as though the Holy One, blessed be He, sits opposite him and reads and studies with him - therefore it says "before the presence [nochach penei] of the LORD," and further on it says (1 Kings 20:29), "and these encamped opposite [nochach] these" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:73: And with this the chapter is concluded, and we have included the particular aspects of speech one must be careful of, according to the shortness of our understanding - and whoever adds further to such fences, may the blessing of good come upon him:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:1: After we said, in the previous chapters, that the matter of speech depends on the mouth, we wish to speak and, connected to this matter, [address] the holiness of eating, which depends on the mouth - for King Solomon, peace be upon him, mentioned the guarding of the mouth in saying (Proverbs 21:23), "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles," and it is explained in Parashat Shemini (Zohar, page 41a-b), whose wording we copied in chapter 11, that "his mouth" means the guarding of his mouth from impure foods. And with God's help we shall explain the aspects of the holiness of eating in what is permitted, according to what is found in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, and the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, and the words of the commentators.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:2: Just as our holy Torah mentions the word "holiness" concerning forbidden relations (Leviticus 20:7), and likewise concerning tzitzit (Numbers 15:40) and other places, as we explained at the beginning of this Gate, so it mentions it concerning foods - and therefore, at the end of Parashat Shemini, having mentioned the permitted and forbidden foods, it says there (Leviticus 11:44), "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy... and you shall not make yourselves detestable." And the Zohar explains this matter, that upon the impure foods the Torah warns us of, an external and impure spirit rests, and therefore whoever eats of these things defiles his soul and shows about himself that he has no part in holiness or in the God of Israel, for the impure thing becomes part of a limb within the person's very body, and the soul clothes itself there - it follows that he defiles his soul and defiles the soul clothed in the body. And through this the wording of the Zohar is precise, saying, whoever eats of those forbidden foods becomes attached to the Other Side and defiles his soul and his body, and an impure spirit rests upon him - and its saying "his soul and his body" teaches what has been said. And they elaborate further there on the punishment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:3: So too, one who eats his food for the sake of Heaven, as shall be explained, and from the things the Torah permitted, upon which rests a spirit of righteousness, holiness, and purity - the soul enjoys that eating from the aspect of holiness within it - and this is (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul." For by the plain sense of the verse it is difficult - what is "to satisfy his soul"? For the soul is spiritual and holy, and is not satisfied by this physical eating but only by the eating of Torah - and so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Beshalach, page 62b), that "his soul's satisfaction" is the spiritual eating, which is the eating of Torah, in these words: it says there that a person should not eat until he has prayed for his sustenance, and they said, of blessed memory, Rabbi Yitzchak said, from here (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - after his soul is satisfied from praying and reading Torah - to this point. Behold, it says "his soul's satisfaction" according to the truth, namely the spiritual satisfaction pertaining to the soul - however, in what we explained, that in the eating itself there is an aspect of holiness, from that aspect of holiness the soul is satisfied.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:4: And therefore it is fitting for a person to be strict with himself concerning his own food, that it have no aspect of prohibition at all - for the prophet Ezekiel would praise himself for not eating from an animal that a sage ruled on, even though it was permitted, since a doubt of prohibition arose concerning it - as they said, of blessed memory, in the chapter "Elu Treifot" (Chullin 37b), on the verse (Ezekiel 4:14), "nor did piggul flesh come into my mouth" - all the more so if there is an aspect of prohibition in the food itself, it is fitting to distance oneself from it. And there are several matters where a dispute arose among the later authorities as to whose ruling is halachah, one forbidding and one permitting - and certainly the prophet Ezekiel, peace be upon him, would not eat such a thing, for the one who forbids it treats it as a piece of forbidden matter, and it is more severe than one on which a sage has [merely] ruled [that it is permitted]. And it is written in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Repentance, chapter 5) that the pious would abstain from seventy gates of the gates of the permitted, out of their fear of one gate of the gates of the forbidden.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:5: And similarly one must be careful in several other matters, not to buy things that carry a suspicion of prohibition except from an honest Jew who is meticulous about it properly - for if he is suspected of it, he is not trusted, as we learn at the end of chapter 4 of Bechorot (mishnah 10): this is the general rule, whoever is suspected of a matter is neither judged by it nor testifies concerning it - and this matter applies particularly to bread, wine, meat, milk, cheese, and grape honey, and anything involving the cooking of gentiles, except what the halachic authorities have explicitly permitted.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:6: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 21:23 - actually 13:25), "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul," several explanations, all coming to one path, in these words: another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Eliezer, servant of Abraham, who said to our mother Rebecca (Genesis 24:17), "please let me sip a little water from your jug" - one sip. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" - this is Esau the wicked, who said to our father Jacob (ibid. 25:30), "let me gulp down, please, some of that red stuff" - that wicked one opened his mouth wide like a camel and said, open my mouth and let it flow in, empty the whole pot into it, as we have learned (Shabbat, chapter 24, mishnah 3), one may not stuff a camel [with a lot at once] nor force-feed it by pressing, but one may pour food into its mouth [to gulp].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:7: Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Ruth the Moabite, as it is written (Ruth 2:14), "and she ate, and was satisfied, and left over." Rabbi Yitzchak said, from this you hear two things - either a blessing rested in that righteous man's [Boaz's] hand, or a blessing rested in the belly of that righteous woman - from the fact that it is written "and she ate, and was satisfied, and left over," it appears that the blessing rested in the belly of the righteous woman. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" - these are the nations of the world, idol worshippers, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:8: Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Hezekiah king of Judah - they said of Hezekiah king of Judah that he would eat two bundles of vegetables, and one litra of meat was brought before him every day, and Israel slandered him and said, this is a king, and Retzin is a king - the delight and kingship fitting for Retzin son of Remaliah - this is what is written (Isaiah 8:6), "because this people has despised the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" - this is Hezekiah king of Judah, who would purify Israel in a mikveh of forty se'ah, corresponding to the numerical value of "le'at" [gently] - the Holy One, blessed be He, said, you bring up food and are satisfied [with little], therefore behold, the LORD brings up upon you the waters of the river. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" - this is Mesha king of Moab, who was a sheep-breeder - and what is "noked"? A shepherd, as it is said (2 Kings 3:4), "and Mesha king of Moab was a sheep-breeder," and so on. And in the Yalkut (Mishlei, siman 950, page 138, col. 2) it is brought in another manner, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is Hezekiah, as stated; "but the belly of the wicked shall want" - this is Pekach son of Remaliah, who would eat three hundred fledgling birds as dessert after a meal - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:9: Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - these are the kings of Israel and the house of David; "but the belly of the wicked shall want" - these are the kings of the East, for whom a hundred sheep would be brought up for each and every one. Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" - this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who said to Israel, My children, of all the offerings you offer before Me, do I derive any benefit from them except the pleasing aroma? - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:10: Behold, it appears from this teaching the virtue of the righteous, who content themselves with little, and the wicked, who are not satisfied with little - and the reason is that their belly is lacking, that the whole world would not suffice to fill their belly, and it appears in their eyes that their belly is never full.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:11: And when a person sees that everything he adds to his eating adds flesh for the worm, which is his end, certainly it is fitting to distance himself from excessive eating except particularly on Sabbaths and festivals - for whoever indulges in eating and drinking on the six weekdays more than needed for the sustenance of his soul and body is punished, and concerning them it is said (Malachi 2:3), "and I will spread dung on your faces, the dung of your festivals." And it is explained in Tractate Shabbat (151b), on this verse - Rav Huna said, these are those who neglect the words of Torah and make all their days like festivals - and it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel, page 199b), whose wording we copied in the Gate of Fear, chapter 12, that after three days his belly bursts, and they throw the dung on his face, and say to him, take what you chose, and made all your days like festivals and appointed times - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:12: And further, they said in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 141a), in these words: the bodies of the righteous, who were not drawn in this world after the pleasures of that strong husk, an impure spirit does not rule over them at all, for they did not participate at all in this world after that strong husk and its pleasures and delights, and they are prepared - such a one is not defiled after his soul departs from him. The bodies of the righteous, who delight in this world only in the pleasures of a commandment and the meals of Sabbaths, festivals, and appointed times - that impure spirit cannot rule over them, for they did not delight in its own [pleasures] at all - since they took nothing of its own, it has no permission over them at all - happy is he who derives no benefit at all from its own - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:13: Behold, it is explained that whoever delights in meals that are not from Sabbaths and festivals delights from the husk, and the husk rules over him at his death - and this husk is the hard husk of the nut, which is the second husk, and therefore it is called the "strong husk," as explained above that the first husk of the nut is soft.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:14: And the reason pleasures are in this hard husk is because everything a person eats beyond the sustenance of the soul is pleasure, and he adds flesh to his body for the worm - and the reason is that according to how much he is drawn after the worm, which is the husk, the husk shall rule over him, for the flesh of the body in man is drawn from the skin of the serpent, as explained in the Tikkunim (page 42), in these words: at the time Pharaoh's daughter touched him [Moses], the Shechinah flew from him, and therefore, when he wished to draw near her at the burning bush, she said to him, do not come closer, until he strip off that body which Pharaoh's daughter had touched - there it was shown to him that a person's body in this world is leprosy from the skin of the serpent; afterward, when he stripped it off and returned to the Garden of Eden, he was clothed in his own holy body, and this is "and behold, it had returned like his flesh" (cf. Exodus 4:7) - to this point, relevant here. And there is no entry for the external force to cause sin except from the aspect of food, for Samael and his groups are spiritual and man is physical, and they have no entry or relation to attach to him - but when a person is drawn after his desire, he gives a portion to his flesh, which is made from a putrid drop, which is from the husk, and through this he causes it to sin - as it says in the Tikkunim (page 53b), that all sins are from the limbs of the putrid drop, and they say there that the putrid drop is an evil maidservant - and therefore it is said in the Sifrei (Ha'azinu, piska 13), as we shall copy its wording below, that a person rebels only through eating and drinking.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:15: And further, they said, of blessed memory, in Berachot (29b): Elijah said to Rav Yehudah, brother of Rav Sala, do not become angry and you will not sin; do not become drunk and you will not sin. Rabbeinu Yonah's disciples explain "do not become drunk and you will not sin" as meaning, and do not become full [sated], so that you not come to sin - for when a person is full and drawn after his pleasures, he forgets the matters of the blessed Creator. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explains "do not become drunk" as, do not become intoxicated with wine - and the law is with him, for the Targum on (Genesis 9:21), "and he drank of the wine and became drunk," is "veshati min chamra u-revi," and likewise "shikor yayin" [drunk with wine] is "meravi chamra" - except that Rabbeinu Yonah's disciples' explanation may also be reconciled, since generally a person only becomes intoxicated from an abundance of eating, when he is full - and thus both explanations are correct.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:16: And further it says in Bereshit Rabbah (38:7), concerning the generation of the dispersion, in these words: Rav Chelbo said, wherever you find satisfaction of spirit, Satan accuses; Rabbi Levi said, wherever you find eating and drinking, Satan accuses - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:17: And in the Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar, Parashat Chayei Sarah, page 127a), it says, concerning the resurrection of the dead, concerning (Genesis 24:4), "but you shall take a wife for my son from there" - Rabbi Yitzchak said, that body which suffered with me in that world and had no pleasure and yearned for it out of fear of its Maker, that body I shall take for Isaac - to this point, relevant here. And from this it appears explicitly that whoever suffers and distances himself from pleasures fears the LORD, as it says, "out of fear of its Maker" - and the intent is that he does not wish to enjoy so as not to come to sin, for pleasure brings one to sin, as we have explained and shall further explain, with God's help. See, see indeed how much one must distance himself from the husk of pleasures and subdue it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:18: And at the end of the teaching it says, happy is he who derives no benefit at all from its own - it changed its wording, for above it said "did not delight" from its own, and here it says "derives no benefit" from its own. And the intent is to inform us that there is an additional virtue for one who has not even a slight benefit from the husk, all the more so pleasure - and this is the nature of the phrase "happy is he" [zakai hu] - meaning an additional, greater virtue. And this is the way my teacher, peace be upon him, followed - wherever the Zohar says "zakai hu," it indicates something more excellent than what preceded.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:19: And its explanation that he has no benefit is that he content himself with a small amount for the sustenance of the soul - and this is "the sustenance of a Torah scholar," which Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Parashat Beshalach, page 62a), whose wording we copied above, "happy is the portion of the body that can be nourished with the food of the soul." And it appears to me that the intent is that that husk, which is the husk of the worm, shall not rule over him - therefore a person must distance himself from this hard husk, which is what causes a person to pursue eating and drinking.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:20: And Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, author of Menorat HaMaor, wrote (part 2, letter 17), in these words: because of the lowliness of his name, the wicked person who pursues eating and drinking is called "Oy Val" [woe and futility], an acronym of "eat, drink, he shall say to you" (Proverbs 23:7) - for he thinks this world was created only for eating and drinking, and those who pursue their desire, today satiate themselves with what is permitted, and tomorrow with what is forbidden - and when they cannot obtain it from their own, they steal from others - and concerning this the Torah commanded the matter of the wayward and rebellious son, that he be killed if his father saw him eat two tartemars of meat and half a log of Italian wine - for since he has begun pursuing pleasures, he shall come to consume his father's property, and if he does not find it, he shall come to rob people - and it is better that he die innocent rather than die guilty - so they said in the chapter "Sorer U-Moreh" (Sanhedrin 72a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:21: Therefore one must be careful not to pursue excesses, for excessive eating is what brings a person to sin, and immediately his inclination becomes proud over him - as they said in the Sifrei (Ha'azinu, piska 13), in these words, on (Deuteronomy 32:15), "and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked" - from satiety they rebel. And so you find concerning the generation of the Flood, that they did not rebel before the Omnipresent except through food, drink, and tranquility - what is said of them? (Genesis 11:1), "and the whole earth was of one language." And so we find concerning the men of the [Tower of Babel], that they did not rebel before the Omnipresent, and so on - and so it says (Ezekiel 16:48), "as I live, says the LORD, Sodom your sister has not done, she and her daughters, as you have done." You find concerning the men of the wilderness generation, that they did not rebel before the Omnipresent except through food, as it is said (Exodus 32:6), "and the people sat down to eat and drink" - what is said of them? (ibid. 32:8), "they have turned aside quickly from the way." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, tell Israel, when you enter the land, you shall rebel against Me only through eating and drinking, as it is said (Deuteronomy 31:20), "for when I shall bring them into the land which I swore to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey, and they shall eat and be satisfied and grow fat, then they shall turn to other gods." Moses said to Israel, when you enter the land, you shall rebel only through eating and drinking, as it is said (ibid. 8:12), "lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses," and so on, "and your herds and flocks multiply" - what is said of them? (ibid. 8:14), "then your heart shall be lifted up, and you shall forget the LORD your God." And so you find concerning Job's sons and daughters, that calamity came upon them only through eating, drinking, and tranquility, as it is said (Job 1:18), "while he was yet speaking, another also came and said, your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine... and behold, a great wind." And so you find concerning the ten tribes, that they were exiled only through eating, drinking, and tranquility, as it is said (Amos 6:6), "who lie upon beds of ivory... who drink wine in bowls... therefore now they shall be exiled at the head of those who go into exile" - and they elaborate further there - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:22: And in the Tosefta of Sotah, chapter 3 (siman 3), they prove all this from the verses concerning the men of the Tower, as it is said (Genesis 11:2), "and it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they dwelt [vayeshvu] there" - and "dwelling" [yeshivah] refers only to eating and drinking, as it is said, "and the people sat down [vayeshev] to eat and drink" (Exodus 32:6) - it was this that caused them, "and they said," and so on. The men of Sodom did not become haughty before the Omnipresent except through the good He bestowed upon them, as it is said (Job 28:7), "a path that no bird of prey knows... a land from which bread comes forth... a place whose stones are sapphires." The men of Sodom said, since food comes forth from our land, and silver and gold come forth from our land, and precious stones and pearls come forth from our land, we do not need people to come to us, for they only diminish us - let us stand and abolish the practice [of hospitality] from among us. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, when I did good to you, you sought to abolish the practice [of hospitality] from among you - I shall abolish the practice from among you and forget you from the world. What does it say? (ibid. 12:6), "the tents of robbers prosper... those who provoke God are secure" - and so it says (Ezekiel 16:48), "as I live, says the LORD, Sodom your sister has not done... behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread," and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:23: And just as one must be careful of excessive eating, so one must be careful of excessive wine - for a little of it benefits the stomach and gives clarity, as they said, of blessed memory (Horayot 13b), "wine and fragrances make [scholars] clear-minded" - but one who becomes drunk with it destroys his body and loses his mind, and it causes him all the evils in the world, as we find concerning Noah, that it caused him harm and disgrace, and became a cause for him to curse his own descendants, as we read in Sanhedrin (70a): the Galilean expounded, thirteen "vav"s [connective "and"s, punning on "vai," woe] are stated concerning wine (Genesis 9:20-24): "and Noah, a man of the earth, began [vayachel]," "and he planted a vineyard," "and he drank of the wine," "and he became drunk," "and he uncovered himself," "and Ham saw," "and he told his two brothers," "and Shem and Japheth took," "and they placed it on the shoulders of both of them," "and they went," "and they covered," "and Noah awoke from his wine," "and he knew what his youngest son had done to him" - to this point. And it appears to me that the intent of these thirteen "vav"s is that they are all "vav-yud" [connective forms], to indicate "oy, vai" [woe, alas], and they are thirteen, to indicate a blemish in unity, for "echad" [one] totals thirteen. And further, thirteen times "vav" totals seventy-eight, corresponding to the numerical value of the three Names "YHVH Melech YHVH," and so on. And there is proof for this from what is said there, further: the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Noah, should you not have learned from the first man, whom only wine caused [to sin]? As they said in the Midrash, that tree from which the first man ate was a grapevine, for there is nothing that brings wailing into the world upon a person like wine - to this point. Behold, it says that the sin of the first man was in it, and they said, of blessed memory, that a taint of disqualification was cast into the first man in that sin - and it says "there is nothing that brings wailing," precise about the language of "vai" [woe].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:24: And further we say there in Tractate Eruvin (65a): Rabbi Chanan said, wine was created in this world only to comfort mourners and to pay reward to the wicked, as it is said (Proverbs 31:6), "give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those of bitter soul." Rabbi said, what is written (ibid. 23:31), "do not look upon wine when it is red, when it gives its color in the cup"? Do not look at wine, which makes the faces of the wicked red in this world, but in the end whitens their faces in the World to Come. Rava said, "do not look upon wine when it is red" - for its end is blood. Rav Kahana raised a difficulty: it is written "yesamech" [without the letter he, defective spelling] but read as "yesamach" - if he merits, it gladdens him; if he does not merit, it makes him desolate - and this is what Rava said, "wine and fragrances make [scholars] clear-minded" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:25: Further, they said in Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 23:29), "who has woe, who has sorrow" - Rabbi Simon said, come and see how severe wine is, that thirteen "vav"s are stated concerning wine at the beginning, and so on, as expounded. And it says afterward, Solomon came and explained in his wisdom, "who has woe, who has sorrow" - this is one who becomes drunk, woe to him and to his father, as it is said (Deuteronomy 21:18), "if a man has a wayward and rebellious son." "Who has strife" - because he becomes drunk with his wine, he reveals a secret between one person and another, and he sows discord. "Who has complaint" - because he becomes drunk with his wine, he speaks excessively, and so on. "Who has wounds without cause" - because he becomes drunk with his wine, he goes and makes a wound and a bruise. "Without cause," why? Because there is no judgment against him [he is too drunk to be held responsible]. "Who has redness of eyes" - one who drank as much as he needed - this is what is written (Genesis 49:12), "his eyes red from wine, and his teeth white from milk" - Rabbi Yirmiyah said, do not read "u-lvan shinayim" [white of teeth] but "lavan sanim" [whitens those who hate him] - just as milk pacifies an infant's mind, so wine restores an elder's mind.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:26: What is written after it? (Proverbs 23:30), "those who tarry long over wine, those who go to seek out mixed wine" - Rabbi Elazar said, woe to him who neglects words of Torah and rises early for wine. What is written after it? "Do not look upon wine when it is red, when it gives its color in the cup [ba-kos]" - Rabbi Yochanan said, it is written "ba-kis" [in the purse] but read "ba-kos" [in the cup] - and why is this? The buyer sets his eyes on the cup, and the seller sets his eye on the purse. And in Vayikra Rabbah (12:1) it explains the completion of the verse explicitly: "it goes down smoothly" - in the end he turns his house into a level plain [ruined] - from this copper pot he makes a clay pot, a servant sells it and drinks wine with its price - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:27: What is written after it? (ibid. 23:32), "in the end it bites like a serpent, and stings like a viper" - just as the serpent bites and kills and separates between death and life, so wine separates between death and life - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:28: Further, they said, "lest he drink and forget mechukak [that which is decreed]" (Proverbs 31:5) - "mechukak" totals two hundred forty-eight, meaning that through drinking wine he shall forget to fulfill the two hundred forty-eight positive commandments - in these words: "lest he drink and forget mechukak" - whoever drinks much wine eventually forgets in his two hundred forty-eight limbs - this is what is written, "lest he drink and forget mechukak" - written "mechukak," and they [total] two hundred forty-eight. Rabbi Chanina bar Papa said, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, I had a great House and destroyed it only because of wine. And the Rabbis say, I had two princes [Nadav and Avihu] and they died only because of wine, for Rabbi Yishmael taught, the two sons of Aaron died only because they entered [the sanctuary] having drunk wine - to this point. "He shall drink and forget mechukak" - Rabbi Shimon said, these are the words of Torah, which are engraved [chakukim], and it is written concerning them (Exodus 20:13), "you shall not commit adultery." Further it says, he shall forget the Torah given through the lawgiver [mechokek] - this is Moses, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:21), "for there the portion of the lawgiver [mechokek] was hidden away" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:29: Further, in Midrash Rabbah, Parashat Nazir (Bamidbar Rabbah 10:2), in these words: "do not look upon wine when it is red" (23:31) - the holy spirit warned concerning wine, that a person not become drunk - why? "When it gives its color" - for its end is blood, that he commit a transgression for which he is liable to death. Another interpretation, "for he shall lust after" the blood of a menstruant and the blood of a woman with a flux. "When it gives its color in the cup" - written "in the purse" - through the cup he shall give his eye to the purse - the Torah spoke in refined language, meaning that he shall come upon forbidden relations. "It goes down smoothly" - in the end his wife says, I saw it like a red rose [i.e., signs suggesting adultery] and he does not separate from her [investigate]. Rabbi Asi said, if he is a Torah scholar, in the end he declares the pure impure and the impure pure. Another interpretation, "it goes down smoothly" - in the end he permits transgressions and treats them as ownerless, like a level plain - he converses with a woman in the marketplace, speaks vulgarly in his drunkenness, and is not ashamed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:30: "In the end it bites like a serpent" - just as the serpent, by enticing Eve to drink wine [i.e., eat the fruit], caused the ground to be cursed because of it, as it is said (Genesis 3:17), "cursed is the ground because of you" - so, through wine, a third of the world was cursed, as it is said (ibid. 9:24), "and Noah awoke from his wine," and so on, (ibid. 9:25), "cursed be Canaan" - this was Ham, who was his third son, and he is called the father of Canaan, and therefore they were cursed. Just as the viper separates between death and life, so wine separates a person from the ways of life to the ways of death, since wine causes him to come to idolatry - this is what is written (Proverbs 23:33), "your eyes shall see strange things [zarot]" - as it is written (Psalms 81:10), "there shall be no strange god [el zar] in you." Another interpretation, that he comes upon a married woman, as it is said (Proverbs 5:20), "and why should you, my son, go astray with a strange woman [zarah]?" - to this point. And from the sum of the teaching you learn that wine causes idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:31: Further there, another interpretation, that it makes the commandments strange, as it is said (Proverbs 21:24), "proud, haughty, scoffer is his name, who acts with insolent pride [za'don]" - this is a drunkard, who is called haughty and a scoffer. "Haughty" - from where? As it is said (Habakkuk 2:5), "moreover, wine is a traitor, a haughty man, and he does not stay home." "Scoffer" - from where? As it is written (Proverbs 20:1), "wine is a scoffer, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" - behold, he is also called a scoffer - and you already know that the group of scoffers does not receive the countenance of the Shechinah (Sanhedrin 103a). Further there, "and your heart shall speak perverse things" (Proverbs 23:33) - for he turns his face away from the Holy One, blessed be He, and from the commandments, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:20), "for they are a perverse generation," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:32: "And you shall be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea" (Proverbs 23:34) - this is Noah, who lay in the ark for twelve months amid the waters of the Flood, and because he drank and became drunk, an unfitness happened to him, that he was castrated [by Ham]. "And like one who lies at the top of a mast" - this is the primordial man [Adam], who is the head of all people, upon whom death was decreed because of wine, and who caused death's pangs to be brought into the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:33: "They struck me, and I felt no hurt" (Proverbs 23:35) - woe to the adulterer who does not learn wisdom from what happened to him - he saw what happened to the "sotah" [suspected adulteress] through wine, and did not learn wisdom. "They beat me, and I did not know it" - he saw in the Torah what happened to the adulterer through wine, and did not know how to understand, but rather said, "when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again" - for as long as he has leisure to occupy himself with licentiousness, he pursues it. Behold, we have learned that wine causes licentiousness, and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, wrote in the Torah the portion of the Nazirite after the portion of the "sotah" - so that a person not do the deed of the adulterer and adulteress, who drank wine and were corrupted, but rather one who fears sin shall make himself a Nazirite from wine - therefore it is said (Numbers 6:2), "if a man or woman shall set apart" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:34: And what we find in the Talmud, "wine and fragrances make [scholars] clear-minded" - this refers to wine in small amount, well diluted; but undiluted wine is what is harmful - and so it is understood there in Midrash Bamidbar Rabbah - see there - and we shall not copy its wording so as not to be lengthy.
